results.title: Tacos El Bronco on Longwood — still the spot?
results.content:
Reply from Bronx_bites_87: Been going to Tacos El Bronco for years now. Still the best al pastor in the borough, no question. The suadero is what keeps me coming back though — that crispy edge they get on the griddle is something else. 

Reply from Marta_nyc23: I've only been once but loved it. Is it still cash only?

Reply from Bronx_bites_87: Yeah cash only, always has been. ATM across the street if you forget. Also worth knowing — they let dogs hang out by the counter if they're well behaved. I bring my little guy sometimes and the guys behind the griddle always toss him a scrap of tortilla. No step at the entrance which is nice for older folks in the neighbourhood, though the doorway is a bit narrow — I wouldn't try getting a wheelchair through there.

Reply from Marta_nyc23: Good to know, thanks! Will check it out this weekend.

results.author: nyc_food_diary
results.title: Tacos El Bronco: Bronx al pastor that actually delivers
results.content:
Tacos El Bronco on Longwood Ave has been on my list for a while after reading about it in a few Bronx food guides. Finally made the trip up on a Friday evening. Got there around 9pm expecting the usual late-night crowd — and the place was buzzing but not stuffed. The griddle was going full blast, that smoky charred smell hits you before you even get through the door.

Ordered three al pastor and two suadero. The al pastor was sliced fresh from the trompo right in front of me — deep red, caramelized at the edges, exactly what you want. The suadero was even better: soft, beefy, almost buttery. Topped both with the green salsa from the bar, which has a serious kick. Hands down some of the best tacos I've had in the city this year.

Important note on timing: they close at 10pm on Fridays now, so don't plan a late-night trip based on older posts you might come across. They've pulled the hours back a bit from what they used to run. I also noticed a couple of people had brought in their own drinks from the bodega next door and nobody minded — handy if you're on a tight budget. Not really a kids sort of place, it's mostly folks grabbing a late bite after work. Cash only as everyone says, and counter seating only, but you're not coming here for luxury. Four bucks a taco and absolutely worth the trip to the Bronx.

results.author: bronx_explorer_92
results.title: Heads up — Tacos El Bronco in the Bronx is the real deal
results.content: Stumbled into Tacos El Bronco on Longwood Ave last Friday night around 10pm. Place was still going strong. Al pastor sliced straight off the trompo, suadero that melts in your mouth. Cash only so come prepared. They're open till 11 on Fridays which is great for a late feed. Tortillas are handmade, salsa verde is legit spicy. Grabbed a quick snap of the griddle but a guy at the counter pointed at a no-photos sign — fair enough, they're just trying to work. Not much seating — just a few counter stools — but nobody comes here for the ambience. Parked right on the street out front, plenty of spots that time of night. Two tacos and a jarritos ran me about $12. Definitely going back.

results.title: Tacos El Bronco on Longwood — still the spot?
results.content:
Reply from Bronx_bites_87: Been going to Tacos El Bronco for years now. Still the best al pastor in the borough, no question. The suadero is what keeps me coming back though — that crispy edge they get on the griddle is something else. 

Reply from Marta_nyc23: I've only been once but loved it. Is it still cash only?

Reply from Bronx_bites_87: Yeah cash only, always has been. ATM across the street if you forget. Also worth knowing — they let dogs hang out by the counter if they're well behaved. I bring my little guy sometimes and the guys behind the griddle always toss him a scrap of tortilla. No step at the entrance which is nice for older folks in the neighbourhood, though the doorway is a bit narrow — I wouldn't try getting a wheelchair through there.

Reply from Marta_nyc23: Good to know, thanks! Will check it out this weekend.

results.author: nyc_food_diary
results.title: Tacos El Bronco: Bronx al pastor that actually delivers
results.content:
Tacos El Bronco on Longwood Ave has been on my list for a while after reading about it in a few Bronx food guides. Finally made the trip up on a Friday evening. Got there around 9pm expecting the usual late-night crowd — and the place was buzzing but not stuffed. The griddle was going full blast, that smoky charred smell hits you before you even get through the door.

Ordered three al pastor and two suadero. The al pastor was sliced fresh from the trompo right in front of me — deep red, caramelized at the edges, exactly what you want. The suadero was even better: soft, beefy, almost buttery. Topped both with the green salsa from the bar, which has a serious kick. Hands down some of the best tacos I've had in the city this year.

Important note on timing: they close at 10pm on Fridays now, so don't plan a late-night trip based on older posts you might come across. They've pulled the hours back a bit from what they used to run. I also noticed a couple of people had brought in their own drinks from the bodega next door and nobody minded — handy if you're on a tight budget. Not really a kids sort of place, it's mostly folks grabbing a late bite after work. Cash only as everyone says, and counter seating only, but you're not coming here for luxury. Four bucks a taco and absolutely worth the trip to the Bronx.

results.author: bronx_explorer_92
results.title: Heads up — Tacos El Bronco in the Bronx is the real deal
results.content: Stumbled into Tacos El Bronco on Longwood Ave last Friday night around 10pm. Place was still going strong. Al pastor sliced straight off the trompo, suadero that melts in your mouth. Cash only so come prepared. They're open till 11 on Fridays which is great for a late feed. Tortillas are handmade, salsa verde is legit spicy. Grabbed a quick snap of the griddle but a guy at the counter pointed at a no-photos sign — fair enough, they're just trying to work. Not much seating — just a few counter stools — but nobody comes here for the ambience. Parked right on the street out front, plenty of spots that time of night. Two tacos and a jarritos ran me about $12. Definitely going back.

results.author: Melissa Chu
results.title: Mighty Quinn's: The East Village Smokehouse That Gets It Right
results.content:
Okay so I finally made it to Mighty Quinn's Barbeque over on 2nd Ave and wow — I get the hype now. I'd been meaning to try this place forever and a freezing Saturday in January finally pushed me to queue up outside. I'm so glad it did because this is some of the best barbecue I've had in the city.

Let me walk you through what I ordered. The brisket — oh man. It comes chopped into gorgeous fatty chunks with a bark that's got that deep black pepper crust, and the smoke ring is textbook. You can taste hickory and a little applewood. It's tender enough that you barely have to chew but not mushy. The pulled pork is a close second, saucy in that Carolina vinegary way, and they give you a generous pile. The burnt ends though are the sleeper hit — little caramelised nuggets of pure beef candy.

Sides-wise the cornbread is sweet and dense with honey butter, and the mac and cheese is the baked kind with a crispy top. The slaw is refreshingly tangy. Portion sizes are fair — about $18 for a two-meat combo that'll fill you up.

This place is super dog-friendly which I love. A couple of people had brought their pups along and the staff brought out bowls of water without being asked. One guy had this floppy-eared hound hoping for dropped brisket. Also good to know — they're totally okay with you bringing in your own drinks. I saw a couple who'd brought a bottle of wine and another guy had craft beers. Nobody batted an eye. I stuck with their lemonade but good to know you can BYOB or bring dessert from elsewhere.

The vibe is no-frills — order at the counter, grab a seat at a communal table, shout over the hum of the crowd. It's not quiet but it feels alive. Like a proper neighbourhood joint. Bottom line: Mighty Quinn's is legit. Definitely my go-to winter comfort spot.

Every time I go back, and I probably go three or four times a year, the feeling doesn't change.

The dark wood interior, those Tiffany-style lamps, the way the waiters call you "Chief" or "Sweetheart" regardless of who you are — it's a time capsule. The room is smaller and more intimate than people expect. Those deep wooden booths, the pressed-tin ceiling, the whole place has this warm, amber glow that just wraps around you. It's cosy in a way no modern steakhouse manages to pull off.

The entrance has a couple of steps up, which always makes me think — it's not the easiest place to get into if you've got mobility issues, and I don't recall ever seeing a ramp. It's a very old building and that's just how it is, but it's something to be aware of.

I usually drive in from Park Slope and I've gotten good at finding parking on Rutledge or Roebling Street after 6 PM when the restaurant traffic dies down. There's a lot nearby too if you don't want to circle.

The bacon — God, the bacon. That thick slab of sweet-smoked pork belly hasn't changed in two decades. Same recipe, same sizzle. My order hasn't changed either: bacon for the table, porterhouse for two medium-rare (for me and whoever I'm dragging along), creamed spinach, German potatoes. The steak comes out on that pewter platter still hissing, and the waiters slice it tableside with this quiet ceremony that feels almost religious.

Is it the same as it was twenty years ago? Pretty much. The prices have climbed — that porterhouse was maybe $70 back then — but the quality hasn't slipped. The staff turnover seems minimal. I saw the same maître d' last month that I remember from my first visit. He's probably been there forty years.

For me, that's the draw. It's not just dinner — it's a connection to a version of New York that's mostly disappeared. Places like this don't open anymore. It's golden, literally and figuratively.

I've been coming here since I was a kid, back when my grandfather would hold my hand as we crossed Houston Street and tell me the same story — how his father brought him here in 1948 after they got off the boat, and the counterman slid over two bowls of matzo ball soup without anyone asking.
